name: Lillooet
confidence_why: Van Eijk 1981 shows contrastive stress (máqaʔ 'snow' vs maqáʔ 'poison onion') that then shifts rightward two vowels at a time under suffixation, Roberts 1993 confirms that the root's stress is unpredictable and lexically listed while the shift is regular, Swoboda 1971 finds no fixed position, and the weight-sensitive trochaic restatement in Caldecott 2009 and the survey label 'penultimate, subject to weight and morphology' from Czaykowska-Higgins and Kinkade 1998 still start from a lexically given stress, so the difference is one of framing, not fact.

catalog_quote: [p.84 sec. 1] In polysyllabic Lillooet words one syllable is stressed. The stress is phonemic, cf. mạ́qaʔ "snow" vs. mạqáʔ "poison onion", ƛ̓ámin "fur" vs. ƛ̓amín "axe". Moreover, the stress is mobile, it can move to a later syllable as suffixes and/or enclitics are added. The matrix for the distribution of the stress is therefore the word with enclitics (proclitics are irrelevant here). [p.85 sec. 2.1] In words with only full vowels, we have the following shift as suffixes or enclitics are added: the stress moves two vowels at a time from the originally stressed one, as long as it does not fall on the last one. ... we will use the term "first full syllabifier" to refer to the stressed full vowel of the root (hence in ʔúxʷalmixʷ the first full syllabifier is u, while in qan̓ím it is i). [p.88 sec. 3] 1. The counting base for the distribution of the stress is (a) the (last) strong syllabifier in a word, or, if there is no strong syllabifier, (b) the first full syllabifier, or, if there is no full syllabifier, (c) the first weak syllabifier. 2. From this base the stress moves two syllabifiers at a time, as suffixes or clitics are added, as long as (a) it does not fall on the last syllabifier in a word, except when the last syllabifier is also the only full syllabifier (here it may move also one syllable); (b) it does not fall on a weak syllabifier (where it would, the weak syllabifier is ignored).
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (4 landscape sheets, two printed pages each, pp. 83-90; text is letter-spaced Acrobat scanned so I rendered the sheets at 110 dpi and read them as images). Sheet 1 right = p.84 'Stress in Lillooet / Jan van Eijk / Mount Currie, B.C.', section 1 Introduction reads exactly: 'In polysyllabic Lillooet words one syllable is stressed. The stress is phonemic, cf. mạ́qaʔ "snow" vs. mạqáʔ "poison onion", ƛ̓ámin "fur" vs. ƛ̓amín "axe". Moreover, the stress is mobile, it can move to a later syllable as suffixes and/or enclitics are added. The matrix for the distribution of the stress is therefore the word with enclitics (proclitics are irrelevant here).' Sheet 3 right = p.88 section 3 'General…
new_statements.rule_in_words: One primary stress per word (domain = word plus enclitics). The root carries a lexically located stress (phonemic minimal pairs; by default the first full vowel, but not always, e.g. qan̓ím). As suffixes/enclitics are added, stress shifts rightward in binary steps from that base (or from the last inherently stress-attracting 'strong' suffix), landing as far right as possible but never on the word-final syllabifier and never on a weak vowel (ə), which is counted but skipped; all-schwa words stress the first vowel; certain cluster consonants and C-shaped suffixes count as (weak) syllabifiers. Net effect: lexical/morphological base plus quantity(quality)-sensitive rightward alternating rhythm with non-finality.
new_statements.secondary_stress: van Eijk 1981 says nothing about secondary stress. Roberts 1993 (held by the project) reports that van Eijk treats secondary stress as entirely predictable and leaves it unmarked, and cites one fieldwork transcription with secondary stress on alternating syllables preceding the main stress (q'ʷəzq'ʷəzílx-kal̓áp type), i.e. trochaic alternation from the base.
new_statements.exceptions: §4 (p.88-89): roots in full vowel + glottalized resonant count as weak before a direct transitivizer; passive -əm is a full syllabifier and may take stress; -tam- is a weak syllabifier and is skipped; §2.2.2 suffix doublets (-ílx/-ləx etc.) depending on whether the suffix can receive stress; §5 enclitics are full syllabifiers regardless of shape, but a single clitic does not attract stress after an all-schwa word; strong suffixes (-ʔúl 'real', -cút reflexive, -úƛ̓) always attract stress, the second of two consecutive strong suffixes winning; fn.3 a few roots have stress on a weak vowel (papláʔ-type reduplications, mạqáʔ).
new_statements.domain_note: Explicitly the phonological word including enclitics ('The matrix for the distribution of the stress is therefore the word with enclitics (proclitics are irrelevant here)', p.84). Data are van Eijk's own fieldwork at Mount Currie (Lower/southern Lillooet) but the paper is framed for Lillooet as a whole.
new_statements.identity_note: van Eijk's 1981 data come from his Mount Currie fieldwork (Lower/southern Lillooet dialect, Lil'wat), though the paper is titled and framed for Lillooet generally; Roberts 1993 uses the same data. Swoboda 1971 and Davis's teaching grammar describe the Upper (Fountain/Fraser River) dialect. Glottolog lill1248 covers both dialects; no separate dialect glottocodes assigned here.

new_statements.quote: [p.17] According to van Eijk (1997:14), "[i]n both roots and root-suffix combinations, assignment of the stress follows two basic tendencies: (1) in words with at least one [full] vowel...the stress falls on the first [full vowel], whether or not that [full vowel] is preceded by [schwa]; in words with only [schwa], the stress falls on the first [schwa]; (2) from the base established by the first tendency, the stress moves two vowels at a time, as long as it does not fall on the last vowel." [p.18] The examples in (4a, b, c) and (5a, b) show primary stress on the initial vowel, which demonstrates that the stress pattern is trochaic and that feet are assigned from left to right. ... In (4d, 5c, 5e) primary stress occurs on the rightmost foot of the word, indicating that the PWord is right-headed. ... Secondary stress, while not marked in the orthography, occurs on the heads of pre-tonic feet. ... stress may not fall on the final vowel or syllable of a word

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement rule as the catalog's van Eijk 1981 statement (stress starts on the first full vowel and moves two vowels at a time rightward, never final) but recast as a predictable, weight-sensitive trochaic system (schwa vs full vowel, moraic coda clusters, non-finality, right-headed word) with named morphological exceptions, secondary stress on pretonic foot heads, prosodic-domain effects and the first acoustic correlates. This supports labelling the type weight-sensitive rather than 'lexical (unpredictable)'; it does not report the minimal pair or the 'strong syllabifier' lexical base that van Eijk 1981 used. Speakers: four Northern (Upper) and two Southern (Lower) dialect (p.93).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the first full (non-schwa) vowel of the root/stem and then, as suffixes are added, shifts rightward two vowels at a time, never onto the final vowel; formally, moraic trochees are built left to right from the first full vowel, the rightmost foot carries main stress, and the final mora is extrametrical. Weight matters: schwa is stressed only when the word has no full vowel (or as head of the final foot in long words), and root-final / lexical-suffix-final consonant clusters count as moraic for stress. Domain-sensitive (PStem vs PWord); prefixes are unstressed except five deictic prefixes (van Eijk 1997:17, fn 23). Acoustically, stressed vowels have higher F0, longer duration and greater intensity (Ch.5, p.132).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes: secondary stress, not marked in the orthography, falls on the heads of pre-tonic feet (p.18); example (9) p.20 shows primary stress on the second syllable and secondary on the first in cluster-final roots; Ch.5 finds the head/non-head acoustic contrast stronger within feet than between primary and secondary stress (p.132).
new_statements.exceptions: Three morphologically conditioned exceptions per H. Davis (p.c.): the circumstantial morpheme, the passive suffix, and diminutive reduplication (fn 19, p.19); five prefixes that take stress (lá-, 7á-, lhlá-, kná-, 7í-) per van Eijk 1997:17 (fn 23, p.22); schwa can receive PWord-level stress in longer words (fn 20); speakers vary in how many consonants a cluster needs to count as moraic (fn 21). Czaykowska-Higgins & Kinkade (1998) are cited as classing St'át'imcets as 'penultimate, subject to weight and morphology' (p.16).
new_statements.identity_note: Caldecott 2009 covers St'át'imcets as a whole, with six speakers: four Northern (Upper: Tsal'álh, Lillooet) and two Southern (Lower) dialect (p.93); Swoboda 1971 is based solely on the Mount Currie 'Original Lillooet' (Lower/Southern) dialect, one informant, and he states the two dialects differ only lexically (p.2). The catalog citation lists Swoboda 1971 as a PhD dissertation; the title page says Master of Arts.

new_statements.quote: [p.8] Two additional symbols ´ and ` written over vowels are used to designate three levels of stress. The symbol ´ indicates a strong or primary stress in the articulation of the syllable containing the marked vowel and this stress is generally in contrast to a weakly stressed syllable, the latter being indicated by the absence of any stress mark. [p.9] Although the frequency of this secondary stress is relatively low - there are approximately eight primary stresses indicated for every secondary stress in the corpus - its structure, like that of both primary and weak stress, is positionally unrestricted. Generally it occurs in polysyllabic words, e.g. ùxʷəlmíxʷ meaning 'Indian'; however, as in English discourse the distribution of this prosody is often determined by the rhythm of the syntactic unit or even the discourse unit rather than simple morphophonemic criteria.

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog's characterisation of stress as not positionally fixed (van Eijk 1981: 'phonemic' and 'mobile'), and adds a secondary-stress level, but gives no placement rule and treats stress partly as a phrase/discourse-rhythm phenomenon. Data are from the Mount Currie ('Original Lillooet', i.e. Lower/Southern) dialect, one informant (Baptiste W. Ritchie), 1969 corpus (p.2).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Three stress levels (primary, secondary, weak) are marked on vowels; primary, secondary and weak stress are all 'positionally unrestricted', i.e. no fixed position is stated, and the distribution of (secondary) stress is often governed by the rhythm of the syntactic or discourse unit rather than morphophonemic criteria; vowel length is subordinate to stress (stressed syllables are longer). No placement rule is given.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes: a secondary level marked with a grave accent, about one secondary per eight primary stresses in the corpus, generally in polysyllabic words (e.g. ùxʷəlmíxʷ 'Indian'), realisation variable (úxʷəlmìxʷ, úxʷəlmíxʷ); the emphatic marker /k'u/ can surface with secondary or primary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None as such; the section stresses variability: the same lexical item may be realised with different stress patterns depending on syntactic/discourse rhythm.
new_statements.identity_note: Caldecott 2009 covers St'át'imcets as a whole, with six speakers: four Northern (Upper: Tsal'álh, Lillooet) and two Southern (Lower) dialect (p.93); Swoboda 1971 is based solely on the Mount Currie 'Original Lillooet' (Lower/Southern) dialect, one informant, and he states the two dialects differ only lexically (p.2). The catalog citation lists Swoboda 1971 as a PhD dissertation; the title page says Master of Arts.

readall_conflicts: The sources agree on the surface facts (stress is mobile, starts on the first full vowel and shifts rightward two vowels at a time, never final; schwa avoids stress; secondary stress exists) but differ on the type label. Van Eijk 1981 (existing statement) calls stress phonemic (minimal pair máqaʔ 'snow' vs maqáʔ 'poison onion') and bases the count on the last 'strong syllabifier', which the catalog read as lexical (unpredictable); Caldecott 2009, following van Eijk 1997, Roberts 1993 and Roberts & Shaw 1994, presents the same placement as a predictable weight-sensitive trochaic system (full vowel vs schwa, moraic coda clusters, non-finality, right-headed word) with a short list of morphological exceptions, and cites Czaykowska-Higgins & Kinkade 1998 classing it as 'penultimate, subject to weight and morphology'. Swoboda 1971 gives no rule at all, calls every stress level 'positionally unrestricted' and lets syntactic/discourse rhythm decide, which is compatible with either label but adds phrase-level variability. Van Eijk 1997 could not be opened, so its own wording is known only through Caldecott's quotations.
